title: Two dreams in a cell
hook: two prisoners ask about their dreams, and Yusuf first speaks to them of the One

segments.voice: Yesterday: prison, chosen, and a man who asked for help not to slip. Your line was the prison was freer. Did you choose the harder right thing? Day sixty-four.

A hospital ward, a barracks, a long night shift: in hard places, people find each other. They talk. They trade stories. They ask each other the questions they'd never ask at home. Two young men go into prison with Yusuf. The Qur'an says they'd noticed something about him: we see you're one of those who do good. And each of them comes to him with a dream. The first says: I saw myself pressing grapes for wine. The second says: I saw myself carrying bread on my head, and birds were eating from it. Tell us what it means. Today: two dreams in a cell.
screen: `PEOPLE FIND EACH OTHER.` → `YOU'RE ONE WHO DOES GOOD.` → `WINE, AND BREAD FOR BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. Yusuf has the answer. And he makes them wait, not to be clever, but because he has something he wants to give them first. He says: before your next meal arrives, I'll tell you. This is part of what my Lord has taught me. And then he tells them who he is: I follow the way of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub. There's Ibrahim again, the one who looked at the stars and loved what doesn't set, weeks ago on this path. Then Yusuf speaks to them tenderly. The Arabic is ya sahibayi s-sijn: my two companions of the prison. Not you criminals. Not you poor souls. Companions. And he asks them a question: many separate lords, or Allah, the One, the Overwhelming? The decision, he says, belongs to Allah alone. That's the heart of it for Yusuf. Before he tells them anything about their future, he tells them about the One. Then he answers, straight. One of you will pour wine for his master again. The other will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter you asked about is decided. It isn't a gentle answer, but it's honest. And then, a human moment. To the one he knew would be freed, Yusuf says: mention me to your master. And the verse says Satan made him forget, so Yusuf stayed in prison a few more years. The Qur'an's word for that stretch is bid', a handful. It doesn't give the number; commentators usually explain it as three to nine. Some good you do, the world forgets for years.
screen: `BEFORE YOUR NEXT MEAL.` · `MY TWO COMPANIONS OF THE PRISON.` · `THE ONE, BEFORE THE FUTURE.` · `MENTION ME — AND HE FORGOT.` · then, large: `START WITH THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share something kind before you're asked. Settle, and breathe. Yusuf gave his cellmates something before they got what they came for. Think of who's sharing a hard place with you right now: a coworker on the same long project, a family member in the same waiting room, a classmate in the same impossible course. What could you give them before they ask? A word of encouragement. A coffee. A sincere compliment. Calling them companion, in whatever way you say it. Pick one person and one thing. If you pray, you can ask to be good company. The bell holds the time.
Two dreams in a cell. Wine and bread, two cellmates, and a prophet who spoke of the One before he spoke of their futures. Today's word.
screen: `TWO DREAMS IN A CELL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: start with the one. Today, in a hard place, begin with what matters most before you get to what's urgent. Day sixty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims often cite Yusuf in prison as a model of da'wa, sharing faith with kindness and honesty; his address "my two companions of the prison" is quoted as an example of gentle speech.

fork.setup: you're Yusuf. two cellmates bring you their dreams and ask what they mean. you know the answers. what do you do first?
options: tell them the meanings right away.
speak to them of the One, then tell them.
tell only the one with the good news.
fork.reveal: he tells them the answer is coming before their next meal, then speaks of his fathers' way and of Allah, the One. only then does he interpret.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 12:39 and 12:41: "O my two companions of the prison."

trapdoor: what you thought: Yusuf was a dream reader.
what it means: before he reads their futures, he speaks to his cellmates, as companions, about the One.
what a scholar hears: sahibayi is dual, "my two companions"; bid' sinin in 12:42 means a few years, and commentators most often explain it as three to nine.

notes: 12:36–42 paraphrased, not quoted. 12:39's question ('are many lords better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?') is paraphrased neutrally as 'many separate lords, or Allah, the One, the Overwhelming?' Confirm this is presented as Yusuf's words in the story, not as the narrator's judgment of anyone.
'Before your next meal arrives' paraphrases 12:37; commentators read it variously (before food comes to you / before the food you're given in a dream is explained). Confirm.
Who forgot (12:42): most commentators say the freed man forgot; some say Yusuf forgot to remember his Lord. Script follows the usual reading.
bid' sinin: 'three to nine' is the common lexical explanation; confirm.

Editor review 2026-10-01: 12:41 says the second man will be crucified (Pickthall: 'crucified'), not just 'executed', so corrected; the 'three to nine' gloss on bid' is now attributed to commentators; cut 'one morning' (not in the text) and the 'in every hard place' sweep.
